blocks.x: Okay, we're doing an interview today at room 104, History Building, Tulane University. Let's see, today is July the 14th, 1960. And I'm going to get everybody's name here. What's your name then?
Almond Hug.

Paul Crawford. Dick Allen. Okay. That makes it easier for the secretary. She knows which voice is which. Almond, let me see. First thing I'd like to start with is just about you, when you were born and where exactly.
Well Dick, I was born on Tulane Avenue, the exact address I don't know. I was born somewhere on Tulane. I was born December the 6th, 1910.
So, were your family musical at all?

Well, to some extent, yes. My grandfather on my mother's side, his name was Schmidt. My name being Hug, family name. My mother's family name was Schmidt. My grandfather played French horn. My grandfather played French horn. And he traveled around with circus bands. In fact, he was hardly ever at home. Grandmother hardly ever got to see him. I understand that he did play with the Christians at one time. To what extent, I just don't know. But I know that the Christian family were neighbors of my grandmother and my grandfather. In fact, Frankie Christian lived right next door to them. Frankie, I believe, was the one that was scheduled to go away with the original Dixon Land Band, wasn't he? I don't know.
I never could get that story.

I don't know. I better not make that statement because I'm not sure. But it seemed that I'd heard that. Frankie came to a sudden end. He died quite young. And I guess that probably was the reason why he may not have gone. I'm not sure about that. But that was the connection of my grandfather and the Christian family. And on my father's side, Jasper Hug, my uncle played drums. He played around in the old Waterville shows in town, the old suburban houses. And, well, my uncle was a Waterville entertainer. He played a little piano. My mother's brother. So, I don't know. I think that about covers the musical background. Outside of my mother, she played a little piano too.
What was your uncle's name then?

My uncle's name was Dewey Schmid. He's at present District Fire Chief of the city. But he also went with the name of Wilbur Leroy. He used to be with the old-time Waterville comedians, Eddie Chittenden and Ralph Nugas and Paul Soipass. They played the old No Name Theater and all the old theaters and the old days. So, he's still around.
He'd be a good person who likes to see, wouldn't he?

My uncle would be very good because he was associated with quite a good number of these old musicians, especially these old piano players that used to play down on, let's see, I believe it was the, on Ramport Street there. It was an old cabaret called, oh, I just can't remember the name of it right now. Was it near Tom Anderson's?
Yeah, it was around there somewhere.

In fact, I think it might have been one of Tom, might have been Tom Anderson's. Because in those days, he worked around those places singing, you know, working with these old piano players. You know, he knew quite a good bit of them. Some called the name of Martinez, the old piano player. And he worked with Buzzy Williams. You know, he worked with quite a number of them. Did you know Martinez? No, I don't believe I did. It seems as though there was a Martinez in the union, an old timer.
And I just don't recall his first name right now. But I know that he played down there.

I don't know if he played on Basin Street, but I know he played at this old club on Ramport. I've heard of him. And of course, naturally, my uncle, Dui Schmid, was quite instrumental in giving me a lot of encouragement. And of course, he was a man of the union. And he was a man of the union, an old timer. And I just don't recall his first name right now. But I know that he played down there. I don't know if he played on Basin Street, but I know he played at this old club on Ramport. I've heard of him. And of course, naturally, my uncle, Dui Schmid, was quite instrumental in giving me a lot of encouragement of playing piano. Because you love that old style of playing.
Now, the people in those previous generations, did they play what you'd call jams?

Well, when I first started playing Dick, I can remember back that I knew a few piano players that played piano. And it seemed as though to me they played the real old ragtime piano. There was a good friend of mine, his name was Edward Bordeaux. I happen to think of him today, since I was coming up to this interview. The last I heard of him, he went to Memphis, and he was living there. But he never did play anywhere professionally. But he used to play a real good ragtime piano. And I used to just look for him to come over to the house. I was about nine, eight or nine years old at that time. And he used to play a lot of these old rags, like Maple Leaf, and all he played. He played all of the old time ragtime things. He played them real well. But he used to just play it for his own amusement. He didn't play it professionally anywhere. I don't know what happened to him. I don't know if he's still living at this time or not. Did he play by ear or straight up? No, he played for music and it was a funny thing. He used to bring all this music rolled up, you know, and he had a band around it. And he'd come in, he'd sit on it. He was the life of the party, but he had to have the music. But he played it real well. I can remember him real good. And then, I guess I must have been about nine, ten years old. I was down on the corner, it was a Mardi Gras day. And there were three musicians, there was a bass player, an alto sax man, and a guitar man. And they were masked, dressed like mammies, you know. And boy they were playing some real fine swing it seemed to me at that time. It didn't seem like ragtime or the old jazz. They were playing something that sounded real, real good, but it had a real good beat. And, well that made my Mardi Gras day complete. I had to go around and follow them wherever they were at that day. And then, there also was a wagon with a real good tailgate band on it. And they had a piano on it. And that really gave me a real lift to it. It really inspired me. So from that time on, I just made up my mind, I was, that was it. I had to follow that particular type of music. Up to that point, of course, we hadn't brought out one I started playing. Well actually my mother gave me a lot of encouragement because she played a little. And she helped me along to learn the notes. She wasn't really a real great piano player, but she could play enough to be able to pick our tunes. She showed me the notes and helped me a bit before I started taking formal lessons. I took from a lady by the name of Mrs. Asset, a very lovely person. She was married to a very well known person. Detective Henry Asset, he was well known in the city. He's since retired. But she gave me a lot of real good formal basic training. But I must admit, I got real balky after about a year. And I must have given her a real bad time because many a day I made her cry. And I didn't want to stick to that particular type of music that she was teaching me. But she kept impressing me how important it was to learn the notes and learn how to play right. And my uncle wasn't helping much either because he was trying to get me on this real jazz kick. You know, and he was showing me how to improvise with that walking bass and faking chords and things like that. And my mother used to run him out the house. But he really gave me a lot of encouragement and helped me a lot in showing me how to fake and play jazz tunes.
How were you when you went to see Mrs. Asset?

I imagine I was about eight or nine years old. I couldn't have been much younger or older than that. And I didn't stay with her too long, about a year maybe a little better. And then I began practicing all these chords and listening to the sounds and getting pointers here and there from different piano players. Of course, I wish I had met Jelly Rule but he had already left. He was a little bit too far before me. And of course I had heard of him and heard of Steve Lewis. I knew, I had heard a lot of good piano players. I knew that jazz music was a little bit too. But it just didn't seem that any of the names registered with me in those days. But I guess it was just like a lot of jazz is made up of so many different people and things that a lot of them get lost in the shuffle. And I guess there were a lot of good men playing that really didn't come into the limelight.
Oh, about your grandfather, did he play by music or was he a faker or both?

Well, my grandfather died when I was real young and I never even got to know him real well. I don't know whether he played by music or whether he was a faker. I never did get to know that. My Uncle Jasper Hug on the drums, he played by music. I know he used to play with quite a number of bands that read music, so I know he read.
And faked too.

Yeah, he faked too. I don't know if he was a real jazz drummer, but I know he was quite an accomplished drummer. I would say that the turning point in my jazz career came when I met Buzzy Williams. Because my Uncle, Dewey Schmid, had a real good acquaintance with him. He knew him real well and told him that he would bring me and bring him out to the house and let me meet him. And I was about 11 years old or something like that, 12 at the time. I must say that Buzzy was really a wonderful person as he is today. He was not like most musicians, like a lot of the musicians in those days didn't want to help anybody. But Buzzy really was out to help anybody that he could. He showed them the little tricks that he had with that tenth bass that he used to use, a little sort of a walking bass, but instead of using octaves he used tenths. And contrary to most musicians' belief that Buzzy wasn't a good jazz man, Buzzy was quite an accomplished jazz man. It was just that his style of playing I think conflicted with bands. I mean sometimes he would interfere maybe with the blowing instruments, and a lot of musicians said that he wasn't a good band man. But he was mostly known as an accompanist for singers, because Buzzy could play on any key. And in those days that was really an accomplishment. B natural, A natural, E natural, F sharp. Keys were no problem to Buzzy. And he could transpose at sight, and that was a great help to singers. But to get back to Buzzy helping me, he showed me quite a bit of things, quite a few tricks that I even started. Still use in my cleaning today. And I'm really very grateful for the help that he gave me.
He showed you the tenth style bass, and that was way back, huh? That was, well, that was back about 1926.
In fact, I think Buzzy was probably a pioneer. They might say that Buzzy was one of the pioneers in that tenth style of bass, because he really employed it to a great extent.
There was a broken tenth, huh?

Yeah, that's right. He used broken tenths. A roll. A roll, a sort of a roll tenth. He didn't use them in his, how would you say, solid striking them simultaneously. In unison. No, he used them in broken, in broken form. That's right. He played a real, real funny style. That's why he got the nickname of Buzzy, because he was really, Buzzy was really a fast guy in these early days. And they got the same people that heard him said that he sort of made a piano hum. That's where he got the nickname of Buzzy.
Looks like they were calling a phone one.
Oh, man, yeah. Who did he accompany?
Who were some of the singers? Do you remember them?

You know, it's a funny thing. I'm ashamed to say this, but I know Buzzy so personally that it seems it's a shame to say that I can't remember his hometown. Buzzy came down here, oh, he's been to New Orleans, I guess maybe 40 years or better. And I can't remember exactly where he came from, and I can't remember some of the names that he worked with. He's worked with some real, but in fact, in recent years, he mentions some fellow by the name of Tommy Lynam. Lynam, huh?
Oh, yeah.
Tommy Lynam, I think. Lynam, or Lynam?
Lynam, I think. Lynam, I think. Like a Lynam.

Lynam, Tommy Lynam. He's a very well-known entertainer, and Buzzy's worked with him as a, you know, as an accompanist. In fact, he wouldn't have anyone else Buzzy with him. But that's been in recent years now, I'd say in the past 10 years or so. Now, I don't know, I can't remember some of the names that he worked with before that. But he's accompanied pretty near every vocalist in the Wallens, and all the big clubs. He worked in all the big clubs like Club Forest and The Silver Slipper, and The Silver Slipper was really the place on Bourbon Street. He was always, he was always the top accompanist for any of those, any of those performers. I remember one trio that Buzzy worked with that was really a great inspiration to me. It was composed of him and Buzzy and Oscar Marco on violin, and Eastwood, Bill Eastwood on banjo. And I used to listen to them, the days when you had the old earphones, you know, and the crystal set. And they used to really play some fine jazz. They played a real rousing spirited type of thing that really, really moved, you know. You wouldn't call it ragtime or swing, but it was really a real good, they played real good fast stuff that really came off real well.
Somebody had recorded Oscar Marco.
Yes, he was a fine violinist. Oscar Marco played really, really great violin. I can remember him playing fine violin. His brother Mickey Marco was a very good pianist too.
Is there anybody that Oscar Marco played like? Anybody that compared with him?

Yes, I would compare Oscar to, I would say that he played along the lines of Joe Benuti in those days. He played that similar type of jazz. I mean, he played a real nice, hot style of violin. Something that you don't hear too much, you know. He played definitely along, I would say definitely along the lines of Joe Benuti. As much as I can remember.
Back to the piano players, are there any others that you remember in that era that were outstanding?

Well, I would say that after I began playing around the suburban movie houses in town, I used to play for silent movies in those days. Played with three pieces. We used to get a dollar a piece a night. We didn't even get our call fair, but I was playing with a violin player by the name of Grasshoff and a drummer, Surpass I believe was his name. We used to go down to the St. Maurice Avenue Theater and play for these silent movies. The silent movies got a bad deal in those days because we were playing Tiger Rag or some other rag and there would be a love scene. In other words, it didn't make any difference what was going on. We were just playing the same type of music, but nobody said anything. So from there, I graduated to the Foyne Dance Hall. Well, that was really a real good deal there because I met Harry Shields, he was playing there at the time. Buzzy Willards, a very good banjo player. It's too bad that you couldn't have gotten him down. He played a nice banjo. And Von Gammon was playing drums. Bill Gillen was playing trumpet. I can't remember. I don't believe we had a trombone. No, I don't think we had a trombone. One reed? Only one reed? I believe so. I think we had just Harry Shields on the clarinet. I don't believe we had a trombone player. A bass player? Can't even remember a bass player. Because you know in those days they kept things down to the bone too, you know. Oh yeah. So they probably didn't have a bass player. But that was a great spot in those days. That was about 1926. And it was a great meeting place for all musicians. And of course, they played five hours without taking a break. There was no such thing as stopping. You had to grab a Coca-Cola and play with one hand and ready to sandwich with the other hand, you know. Well, let's see. We played four tunes. I believe we played what was called a slow drag. Well, that was the feature dance of every set. When the announcer would say, get your tickets for the four-minute slow drag, all the customers would gang up for that slow drag. Because that was a slow, that was a long dance, you know. They got their money's worth. And we did a sort of a fast tune and a medium tune. And then we did a waltz. Well, on the waltz, the piano player kept playing. But the balloon instruments would get a little, would get a little rest and the waltz would last about two or three minutes, I guess. So that was the extent of their break. Then we went right back over and started playing, playing the fast tunes again. So everybody would always be looking to see somebody come into place, you know. If it was a piano player or a trumpet player or a clarinet player. They'd get them, come on up. Give me a, sit in. Give me a break. So really we had some of the finest men in the business that would stop in there in those days. Like Shawty used to stop in. Eddie Miller would come in. Fazzola would come in. Oh, just can't think of all the guys. They'd all stop in some time or another. He asked me about piano players. There was a piano player by the name of Von Heck that used to play in those days. I don't know what happened to him. He was a pretty good, pretty good man. And there was another piano player by the name of Ernest Baubach that played piano in those days. I followed him in there, I think. Ernest Baubach? Ernest Baubach or Baubach. I'm not sure as to the exact pronunciation now. And they had of course this piano player by the name of Bill Voorhees. He used to play there. He was a good man. Well, I stayed at the firm for about six months or a year. And I say that I got a good foundation there. Because when I came on the job, I had a few tunes rolled up, you know, a few of the jazz tunes written out, you know. And Von Gammon says, oh, what are you doing with that? He says, you're not going to use any music here. He says, besides it's too dark. He says, you'll never be able to read it. I said, well, how am I going to play? He says, well, we'll show you. Well, I think that's an interesting point there, Dick, to bring out, is how jazz was really started in those days. Because the old timers didn't believe in any music. If you had music on the job, you were a square, strictly a square. You better leave that music home. And Harry Shields was sitting right alongside of me. And I said, how am I going to play this tune, Harry? I never heard of it. I think it was That's A Plenty or Clarinet Long Way or something. Harry says, don't worry about it. He says, you'll learn the chords. Well, boy, I really, on the first couple of times, I must have really hit some dillies. Because Harry gave me some real mean looks, you know. So, I was kind of a little disturbed about it. In fact, Harry kind of made me a little peeve there for a while because he was kind of getting on to me, you know, about the chords I was using. But really, it was really a great thing that he did because, I appreciate it because he taught me the right chords, showed me what I should play. And when I got finished there, I knew most of the old tunes.
Would he sit down at the piano?

No, he'd just tell me, well, as we were playing, he'd say, I use F chord next to an A seventh, next to a D seventh here, a D minor, you know. As we were playing, he'd call them out to me, you know. And, well, as I went along, I gradually got to learn the right changes. And then, the melody, you know. But usually, it was usually the chords. I think you brought out a point right before the interview, Dick, about what part the piano played in those days in the band. Because it was kind of lost. Well, of course, the piano, as always, was used as more of a background instrument in those days, and used mostly as a foundation for the blown instruments. And it wasn't too important to play a melody. In fact, the piano man in those days really didn't even have to be a real great soloist. As long as he could play good chords and give a good solid beat and not interfere with what the blown instruments were doing, he was considered to be all right. Of course, if a man could, if a piano man couldn't take a good solo, well, they let him take it. They let him feature a solo. But he didn't have to be a great soloist in those days. And also, just to be a good rhythm man, that was most important.
What kind of rhythms would you use in that?

Well, we used more or less of the old two beat, you know, the strong beat. The strong beat, rather, was in the second beat. I was taught in those days that the first beat on the bass, you know, shouldn't be too heavy, should be exaggerated too much. But that second beat should be the predominant beat. Because they believed in that strong after beat, that strong second beat, you know. And the first beat would be sort of not as strong as the second beat. And that, that, that, that was employed, I employed that type of playing mostly for the first few years that I played. Until later on, we fell into more of a, of a straight four. But we still accented that second beat, where they, where, where I think that the, the term two beat music came in, came in, you know what I mean? They used that, they used that word two beat. But even when playing a four, we still accented that second beat a little bit, which gave it, gave it the impression that we were playing two beat.
Well what notes would you play with your left hand and what with the right? Would you just, would you play a full chord with your left hand?

No, no, no. Usually we played, in fact we could even play, we could even play, oh in fact, this point right here, I'm glad that you reminded me of a piano player, I mustn't forget Freddie. Freddie Newman. Because Freddie Newman was a very, very fine band, played great, great rhythm, because he had been playing with the remnants of the Rhythm Kings, you know. I don't know if he played with the, with the early Rhythm Kings, but I know he was playing at the ringside with Chink Martin and Joe Caprera and Shawky in those days. And I remember Eddie Miller and I, we used to go around and listen to that band, and I used to admire Freddie's, Freddie's orchestra playing. And in fact, he used, he used to use single notes in the bass sometimes, because Chink used to use the sousaphone, you know. And it was so, so, so predominant that, that really you didn't have to have a strong bass on the piano. He didn't even play single notes, play like a, like a major, like a tonic, you know, an F. If you're playing in the key of F, you play F, C, F, C in the bass, with just one finger. And it was very effective. You didn't even have to employ an octave. In fact, an octave was only used maybe if you didn't have a bass, to make it a little more, bring it out a little bit, make it a little stronger, you know. In fact, this, this, this tune zero was something, was something that I learned then. I used, I used to use single notes in the bass because the introduction is . . . Well, that, that, that, that was a famous old, old sousaphone thing that Chink Martin used to do there. And the piano would take, in the, in the absence of a sousaphone, the piano would often take that . . . Just single notes. And it was very effective.
They seem to swing sometimes, you know. Oh yeah. In a way, a single note, something simple like that would really swing.
In fact, it'll swing sometimes even more so than playing, playing octave, octave, octave chords, octaves in, in the bass.
Did many of the guys use octaves? Who would, who would, uh, draw that?

Well, yeah, I guess, uh, I guess so. In fact, I used octave bass, uh, bass, uh, until the time I started doing solo work. And, uh, I'd, I'd vary, you know, use octaves sometimes, and use single note bass too sometimes. Uh, I, uh, the, the type of work that I did, uh, in the, in the orchestra work was, uh, more so, uh, just chord, uh, just an octave in the bass, and, uh, chord in the right hand, using that strict one, two, one, two, one, two, you know, that sort of type of umpah rhythm.
Alternating your hand.

Yeah, that's right. That's right. It was more or less, uh, if you got a good banjo player, and a good drummer, uh, all, all you'd have to do was just, just work right along with that piano, work right along with that, that, that, with that octave in the bass, or a single note, as I said before, and with a, a chord in the right hand, using mostly a tonic. Because, in those days, we didn't use any fancy chords. We didn't use any of those flatted fifths, and those progressive harmonies that they use in the day. We used the bass, straight, basic chords, which is the pure form, and which is the real, real beautiful form of using straight harmonies in, in, in, in jazz music. Uh, as I said before, a, a, a straight, a straight rhythm, with a good banjo playing the four beats, because the banjo would carry, would carry a four beat, accenting that second beat a little bit, you see? Because most, they, they, they all leaned on that second beat. That would, that, that, that, that, that's what they called really giving it a lift. Of course, the drummer would sort of give that same, that same beat using four, but using, accenting the second beat. And all the piano had to do would be to come in there and play the octave and the, and the chord in the right hand. Let, let, let, let him, let him, let him, in other words, I think more or less a piano went to support, to the banjo and the drums. In other words, he shouldn't, he should never have interfered or tried to stand out. I mean, more or, more or less what they wanted the piano there were, or in the old days, was just to be felt. Just know that it's there and that's, that's, that's it. Of course, in later days when Earl Heinz came in with his piano, well, he, he began really revolutionizing that form of playing, and, and, and, and, and brought out the piano more in the orchestra than it had been heard ever before. With his fill-ins and his intricate, intricate passages on, on, on the piano. Of course, I think, I think Jelly Roll did a lot of, a lot of standout work on the piano too. Uh, because Jelly Roll didn't stick to too much of that, of that old stereotype, uh, umpah type of piano. Although he did, I think when he was playing strict orchestra work, he did. Because on some of the old Rhythm King's records, I noticed, I noticed that, uh, you don't hear Jelly Roll trying to stand out too much. He stuck more or less to straight rhythm, unless he was taking a solo, you know. Of course, with his trios, well, he stuck, he stuck out quite a bit.
I wanted to ask you something about that trumpet player that was playing in front of you, Bill Gillan? Bill Gillan?

Bill Gillan was a very fine, very fine trumpet player. Played very, very good, uh, lead trumpet. Um, I think, uh, Bill, Bill, uh, would have been a really, a real fine, all-around, New Orleans man. Uh, of course, he gave it up. I don't know, he hasn't played for quite some time now. In fact, I don't think I've seen him probably ten years or so. Uh, Bill, Bill used to like Bix quite a lot in those days. Uh, in fact, he, uh, he imitated some of his solos quite well. And, uh, we used to kid him to the extent that we used to call him Bix sometimes, you know. He, he had, uh, a couple of solos that Bix did on jazz and blues down. He did, he did him quite well. But, uh, aside from imitating Bix, Bill was, uh, was a pretty good, uh, pretty good trumpet player in his own right.
When did he, uh, die? I mean, when did he stop playing?

Well, uh, far as I know of, he's still living. Mm-hm. But, uh, Bill, Bill's been out of the business, I imagine. I don't think Bill's played the past 25 years that I know of. He just, just quit playing all together, far as, far as I know. Unless...
Okay. That's a new name to me. Bill Gilliam, yeah. He was, he was pretty good, too.
Bill Bander when he took a... Yeah. ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...
Bill Gillen, you say he stopped about 25 years.

I would imagine so, Dick, unless he played around with small bands, maybe spot jogged around, that I never got in contact with him after that because I don't know if Bill ever belonged to the Musicians' Union. He may have, but I don't believe he did. So therefore, after I joined the union, actually, I got out of contact with him. But I don't believe that Bill played much after that.
Whose band was it at the Fern, anyway?
It was Von Gammon's band, the drummer.
And what other bands did Gillen play with that you know of?

I don't know of any other bands that he played with, Dick. The only time that I had ever played with Bill was at the Fern Dance Hall. After I left the Fern Dance Hall, I'd like to mention that I went to my first nightclub job, or cabaret they called it in the old days, was the Valencia on Bourbon Street. That was about 1927, I think. And I played with a little outfit there. I believe it was Hilton Lamar's brother, Jimmy Lamar, played alto sax. And Chink Martin's son, Chink Junior, played banjo. Buck Rogers played drums at one time with us. And then after Jimmy Lamar left, we got Eddie Miller. That was the first time I'd ever played with Eddie. Eddie played outdoor saxophone in those days. We started working at 11 o'clock at night. We got off about 6, 7 o'clock in the morning. I don't think Eddie Miller was ever on time. One time, he was quoting his wife at that time. He'd get to work about 12 o'clock at night. He always had some good excuse though why it was late. The boss never seen the mind. But even in those days, Eddie was playing great saxophone. He always had that nice tone, good ideas, good taste. It was really enjoyable working with that little combo. In fact, I followed a good piano player in there too. Speaking of piano players, I had a good man playing there. He's a very, very, very wonderful person. He comes up to the jazz club meeting sometimes. I know his name as well as I do. Where does he live? He's a barber. Across the river? I think so. Hal Maranto? Hal Maranto, yeah. He was playing piano there at the time. I followed him. In fact, I followed him on the job. And I worked at the Valencia there for quite a while. As I said before, we had, let's see, Jimmy and Eddie Miller and Chink Martin Jr. and Buck Rogers. I don't remember if Emmet Rogers played drums there or not. But I stayed on that job quite some time. And the next job that I can remember came at the old Slipper, the Silver Slipper with Abbie Brunas. Abbie was playing trumpet there. And Emmet Rogers was playing drums in that band. And Sidney Ayrton was playing clarinet. And in fact, Sidney and Eddie Miller were both playing in that band. Eddie was playing alto and Sidney was playing clarinet. And I'll tell you one thing, Sidney played a fine clarinet. Didn't read a note, but sure played great clarinet.
I wonder where he got his style. I can't imagine.

I can't imagine because he certainly played different than anybody that I'd ever heard. He didn't sound like rap. He didn't sound like anybody that I'd ever heard of. You hear other people that sound like him now. Yeah, that's right.

And Sidney never gets any credit for it. He never gets any credit for it. But he sure did play a nice tone. He had a good, beautiful, beautiful tone and wonderful ideas. Well you know he had wonderful ideas to write a tune like Blazy River.

That's just an idea right there of some of the ideas that he had. I followed a piano player in there you're talking about. I know you've known since I'm on the subject of piano players. I know you want to bring out some of the old names that Warren brought out. I'm trying to think of a fellow there that played piano with Abbot Murness at that time. He was a real fine guy. One of these real comical sort of guys. Always wanting to improve his playing. Never did get to be real great but he was a real ambitious sort of guy. Every time you'd get around him he'd start talking about different methods and different books and how to exercise your fingers and he'd be on the streetcars practicing. People thought he was out of his mind and he'd be practicing exercises on his legs. I wish I could think of his name now. I'd sure like to bring his name out. Oh, come to him. Right at this time I thought of another fine piano player. I don't know whether his name has been brought out or not. Red Long. Of course I imagine his name might have been mentioned with the old Halfway House Orchestra. He made some fine records with Abbot Murness. That was when my brother-in-law Joe Lloyd Canner played Algo Saxonwood records. I think my brother-in-law Freddie Lloyd Canner played some guitar banjo on those old records. I'm not quite sure but I believe he did.
See, he sang on some too, Red Long. I don't know if Red sang on them.
I know my brother-in-law Freddie sang on some of those records.
Freddie sang on some of them?

Red had some beautiful tunes that he wrote. I want somebody to love and a few of those, like a, in fact I was playing one of them just the other night. It's a shame that he never did get to do anything with those tunes because he was quite a composer. And played some, played very nice piano too. He's a good piano player. Still trying to think of that piano player that played with Abbot Murness.
He was after Red Long.
He was right around that time. I believe he was before Red Long.
Did you ever know Bill Whitmore?
Bill Whitmore?
Yeah, I'm a fly.

Dick, my memory is a little hazy right at this spot. I remember that name. Oh yeah, Bill Whitmore, sure. I remember him. He was a sort of a stocky, chunky little fellow. Sort of like on your type. He was kind of a little heavy set like. I remember Bill Whitmore, yeah. I do very well now. The first time I thought of him in a good while.
He died over in Florida. He did, yes.
I didn't know that. He wrote that New Orleans Shuffle, you know.
That's a wonderful thing. I like that. Yeah, Bill Whitmore was considered a good piano player.
Do you remember who he played with? No, no Dick. I really, really don't.
I can't remember who Bill Whitmore played with. But now that you mention the name, I know he rated very high in town, yeah.
There's no man. Yeah, that's right. They're quite a good guy. I don't know.
I don't know. There's no man.
Yeah, that's right. They're quite a good bit of men. That names have never been known.
There's a fellow called Zimmerman, who is not related to Roy. He's supposed to have played Ragtime back around, Urban Laclaze time. Uh-huh. Did you ever know him, Tom or Tony? I can't remember.
No, I don't believe it.
He's kind of lost.
Uh-huh.
Tony Parani, I think, said he worked with him.
Uh-huh. What about Erwin Leclerc?
Did you hear him? Erwin Leclerc?

I can't say that I ever remember hearing Erwin play, but I can tell you a funny story about Erwin. Erwin wrote quite a bit of nice tunes. I knew one tune called It's Too Late to Be Sorry. He wrote it with Joe Huertas. I don't think anybody ever played it. Erwin Leclerc. Erwin Leclerc. Erwin Leclerc. Erwin Leclerc. Erwin Leclerc came in there and he knew me and I knew him, but he didn't know that I knew this tune and I started playing it for him. And you should have seen the expression on his face. He came up to me and says, my God. He says, I didn't know anybody ever played this tune anymore. He was so happy about it, he gave me a $5 tip.
Do you still remember that?
Yeah, I still play it.
I think you played it from the other one. It's a good tune.

It's a wonderful tune. In fact, I recorded it for Cosmo Matasson, Ace Label. I'm still waiting for that album to be released right now. You know, knowing Cosmo, I don't know when it'll be released, but he says that it will be released sometime. It's been two years now since I recorded it.
Who were some of those songwriters around that you remember?

Well, as we just mentioned, Erwin certainly wrote quite a number of good tunes, Triangle Rag and It's Too Late to Be Sorry. Joe Voyager, of course, wrote some nice tunes. Don't Leave Me Daddy and Bungalow of Dreams. That's a tune that I don't think too many people play, but I remember it well because Bix Baiderback made a nice record on it. Bix and Trumbau made a fine record on it.
Never heard that.
It's real nice. Well, I mean, it wasn't one of those real jazz tunes, but Bix took a nice little solo on it. It was a real nice little tune. You still play it? Yes, I play it.
I still play it. In fact, I play Don't Leave Me Daddy too.

That's something that you don't hear too many men playing today. You're in jail. It's a good tune. Speaking of composers, there are so many of them like Pierone and Clarence Williams. Of course, I still play a lot of Clarence Williams' tunes. In fact, he had that publishing house on Tulane Avenue on the 1300 block. And he was in the I'm going to have to dig up the files on my birthplace. I might have been somewhere around that way that I was born. I know it was on Tulane Avenue somewhere.
Maybe you heard him playing and got it.
Could be possible. I know I play his Wildflower Rag quite a lot, and that one was published on 13-something Tulane Avenue.
Who are some of the other composers that you remember hearing or talking to around you? For example, did you know Uncle Sammy Rosenbaum? Sammy Rosenbaum, yeah.

I knew Sammy quite well. He wrote a tune with Joe Burgess too. I've got the music home, but I can't remember the title. I wish I had it right now. But I remember seeing his name on the tune with Joe Burgess. And I'm sure that must be him, because it says Sam Rosenbaum.
Oh, yeah. And Clancy, did you know Clancy?

No, I didn't know Clancy personally. I know his niece. His niece often claims that her mother played that tune, It's Too Late to Be Sorry, that's Joe Burgess, I'm Sorry I Made You Cry. She said that her mother had that tune before her uncle had it. Of course, that starts one of those controversies again as to who it really belonged to, you know. But I never did meet, that was Joe Clessie, wasn't it?
No, no. Nick and Jay.
Nick Clessie, that's right. Nick Clessie, yeah, that's right.
Joe Clessie was somebody else.
Joe Clessie was another one, yeah. I don't know if he was in any relation to Nick.
I don't know, I don't have any idea.

I don't know. Did you work with Joe Clessie? No, but I believe my brother-in-law, Freddie Lloyd Cannon, said that he used to play some jaffers with him. I don't remember him ever playing any jaffers with Joe Clessie.
It's supposed to have been quite a band. Yeah. Francis Murray tells some real great stories about this band that worked with him a lot. Supposed to have been a great guy.

Well, the composers, speaking of the composers, Nick, Red Long was really one of the prime composers that I know of. And, of course, I don't remember too many of the other piano players that were composers outside of Joe Burgess and Earl and Claire. I can't think of any piano players offhand who were composers. Of course, we all know, you know, Pierre-Hong, or Pierre-Hong. Steve Lewis wrote some nice stories.
You didn't know Steve Lewis?
I don't know.
I don't remember knowing Steve. He must have been just a little bit before my time, I believe. Well, Harry, Sujohn remembers him well from Victor's.

Well, Harry should, because I'm the same age as Harry. And I should remember Steve, too. Maybe I heard him playing. Like I say, you know, when you're a young kid coming up, you get around, and in those days, it was just a little bit different. I mean, you'd hear a guy and you wouldn't even know who he was. I mean, you'd just know, well, he played good. And probably I did hear Steve playing, because I heard quite a number of fine guys playing piano, and never did get to know who they really was.
What about Perranti? Did you go around and listen to his band ever?

Perranti, yes. I can remember Perranti when he played at the Liberty Theater. He was a big man in those days. All the women and all the girls and everybody used to be running behind him, because he was really a real handsome looking guy, and played fine clarinet in those days. And I believe Perranti had a band at the La Vida, didn't he, at one time? That was right next door to the Fern Dance Hall. And we used to listen, we used to go next door, whenever we got somebody to sit in and play for us at the point, and we'd listen to his band, the La Vida. And I think he had a piano player with him by the name of Dave Lewenta. He was from, I forget where he was from, but he was a fine piano player. He's in Chicago now.
Yeah, David Lewenta.
That was at the pump room you played last?
Yeah, he was at the pump room for years.
I don't know if he's still there or not, but he was a very, very fine piano player. Yeah, Tony Perranti, he used to listen to him quite a lot.
Do you remember Vic Lebowski?

Do I remember Vic Lebowski? Oh, I took lessons from Vic. After I left Mrs. Asap, as I told you, I began just going out on my own, you know, and learning the jazz tunes and learning how to play jazz. But then after a couple of years I realized that I should improve a little bit on my technique and knowledge of music. So I started taking lessons from Vic, and I took about six months from him, and he really helped me quite a lot. But I never, I just couldn't get away from the unorthodox playing. In fact, Vic used to laugh at a lot of things that I do. He'd say, I don't understand how you can do that. He said, you're doing it all wrong, but somehow or another it comes out. And I think that's a good point to bring out in jazz right here, Vic, is the fact that jazz musicians did in those days unorthodox things that came out real good. And in fact, Vic's, you know, played a lot of things that were unorthodox, but they came out so, so wonderful. And I guess Louis Armstrong and all the old trumpet players and old musicians, in fact, we know Rapola must have done a lot of unorthodox things, but they came out so, so fine. I think that's one of the great things about jazz is that you don't have, you don't have to follow the letter on it. It comes out so great.
Vic was a kind of a legitimate guy?

Yeah, Vic was a strict technician. I mean, he did things that I just couldn't believe that could be possible. I remember one day I brought him a copy of Rhapsody in Blue, and it had just come out then. And Vic had never seen that tune. This was just an example of his musicianship. I've been trying to play the doing thing for over 30 years now, and I still haven't played the whole thing through. And I'm telling you, he stood there, he sat down with that copy, the original copy. I mean, nothing left out, and played it from cover to cover. Right before me there, he did leave a thing out. And believe me, that's something. That's the kind of... That's sight. That's sight, he played that thing note for note. That's the kind of a musician he was. Didn't miss a thing. How did he play in the band?
In the band?

Well, Vic was really an exhibitionist at the piano. He was all over the piano all the time, and he always wanted to display his technique. And he never missed an opportunity to let people know how much he could do. But he had something to go on, because he could really do it. He really played a great... In fact, I wouldn't classify Vic as a real great jazz pianist, but he certainly was a great technician. Certainly had a wonderful technique.
Who did he play with?

Well, he played at the Little Club. He had a band up there. I don't know if he had Tony Papalia playing up there with him. I just don't remember the exact combination that he had up there. And then he played at the Sanga. That was one of the feature spots that he played in the days when the Sanga had stage shows. He was a great standby there. In fact, he did lots of solos on the stage. They let him do lots of solos. Yeah, he was one of the real fine piano players around here. Another fine piano player was Howard Tiff. He played at the Alphine Theatre quite some time. I took some lessons from Howard too. Howard was a real fine, legitimate piano player. He could play almost anything too. And there was another fellow by the name of Don Chase. Don Chase played piano at the same time as Vic did at the Sanga. Of course, Don was kind of lost with Vic up there because Don was just a sort of a second piano to Vic. But he was a great piano player in his own right.
Were these guys jazz musicians? Captain Chase?

Well, I guess they probably played with dance bands. Let's put it this way, that they played with dance bands. I wouldn't know what he would exactly call them real jazz musicians because as I said, they were more or less legitimate. Readers. But I guess they did play with dance bands. There was another fellow by the name of Wilson that used to play piano. I think he played at the Lowest State. I can't think of his first name now. But he was quite an accomplished musician himself.
So many of them, you learn new names every day. Yeah, that's just it.

There were many names. But as you said before, Dick, I think that's a good thing to think about. While we're talking about these fellows, I don't know if you would say that they were all real jazz piano players. That is, in a real jazz sense. They may have been able to play with dance bands and play, but I think that they were more or less, most of some of these names that we mentioned, they were legitimate musicians. They played more or less by music, strictly. I don't know if they even played, if they were even able to fake. Because most of those old time musicians that read, they weren't too good at faking music. That gave a guy like me an advantage in those days. A lot of other guys that were coming up that could fake. I'll never forget, I was playing out at, I had a chance to go to work at Old Suburban Gardens in 1931 or 1932, I think it was. Johnny Detroit had the band out there. And there was a piano player playing out there then by the name of Wilbur Dinkle. There's another name. Now Wilbur Dinkle was a fine musician. Not too great a jazz musician, but he could read quite well. And I had the chance to take his place, he was leaving. And came out there and oh, there was some terrific act. There was a show going on and it was a terrific act. And they were playing this Mexican hat dance. And it was written in all sharps. A natural, B natural, F sharp. So Johnny Detroit put the music up, they gave it past the music out, you know. He counted off the beat. Well I got about two, I got about past three measures in that thing. And that was it, I was lost. So Johnny Detroit came around, he says, did you play in that, were you playing in that thing? I says, well Johnny, to tell you the truth. I says, no, I said, I played the first three measures. I said, after that, I said, I was lost. He says, well that's the trouble with you jazz musicians. He says, you see, when you get a chance to play something legitimate, he says, you can't do it. Well you see, there was a good example right there of the line between jazz musicians and legitimate musicians in those days. But Johnny was pretty nice about it. He says, well let's see what we got, let's see what we got coming next. He says, there was a girl singing. And she wanted to sing, I think it was Hussari Now. Well she didn't have the music for it. So she came to Johnny, she says, I want to do Hussari Now. Johnny says, have you got the music? Because Johnny was that way, you know, the acts had to have the music. So she says, no I don't have the music. He says, well how are we going to play it? So I told Johnny, I says, well I know it. I said, if you want to let me play it, I said, maybe some of the other guys know it. He says, well go ahead. So I ripped off an introduction for her and key, whatever key she wanted it in and started playing it. So the girl was so pleased about it that I could play it and a few of the other guys joined in and we faked it through. She says, well that, she says, that was real great. So Johnny Detroit says, well he said, you know something? He says, I got to give you credit kid. He says, you did a good job on that. He says, you know what you do with this other two? He says, take it home and woodshed it. He says, and maybe we can get through it. So I did. I took it home and woodshed it and came back and we played it. So you see, Dick, there was a good example. I'm glad I thought of that point. I mean, that was a good example of what the old musicians had to contend with, you see. In other words, we learned to play tunes, as I said, Harry Shields said, let's swing. We learned, we don't need any music on this. And we were content to go along and just play without music. But of course, there came a time when, if you had to play theater music or show music, that you did have to know something about reading music. And that's where a great line was drawn. But once again, I'm going to say that I kept studying. I said, well, I'm not going to be left behind. I said, I want to keep up with what's going on, you know. And I think that's a good thing for musicians to know how to read. I think that helps out quite a bit. I don't think that it should be that you don't know how to read music at all. That was a mistake that the old jazz musicians made.
What about Louis Armstrong? Did you hear him when he was at the Samaritan Gardens?
Well, let's see. Yes, I did. That's right. He followed, in fact, I think he came in there a little bit later after this band that I was telling you. Yes, I remember hearing Louis out there.
I was trying to establish that date. I think he was there in 31, so you were quite young.
Well, yes. And it could have been possible that Louis played there after or before. I don't quite remember, as you said, that date. But it was somewhere right around in that time.
You must have had a lot of teachers. We haven't covered them all.

Well, let's see. The teachers, we started off with my mother, primarily. I can't forget her. And then my uncle, Duy Schmid, he helped me out with a lot of the faking part of it. Buzzy Williams. I had another fellow that played fine piano with, speaking of piano, his name was Emile Schindler. He never did play professionally, but he used to play very, very fine ragtime piano and good legitimate piano. He helped me out a little bit. Emile Schindler, and then I took from Vic Lebowski, Howard Tiff, Madame Eugene Schaffner, who was certainly excellent. She helped me quite a lot. And then Madame Eugene Schaffner's niece. It was Voltaire, I think was her name. I just don't remember quite. I think it was Voltaire, something like that. It was Madame Eugene Schaffner's niece. So, Dick, I think that about covers all my piano teachers. Quite a variety, yeah.
Quite a variety.

And, of course, I can't forget Vic's Beiderback, the time that he taught me in the middle of the and he taught me in a mist. I can't forget that. That was a lesson that was really a great lesson. Of course, I met him out at Paul Merez's house when Vic was in town with Paul Whiteman. And I would say that covering piano teachers would go back to listening to different piano players. You listen and you learn. And I think that's the way most of the old timers did. They listened and they learned. And one thing about the old musicians, they weren't too proud to be able to try to learn or get somebody to help them.
Kind of like a Wausau just played for fun. They just go around and listen and pick up things. That's right.

I would say my association with Buzzy Williams was really great. And then playing around the spots, being associated with fellows like Chink Morton, old timers like that. They really helped to a great extent. Harry Shields. I met Leon Rapolo one time when I was at the Valencia. And he sat in and played. But he just played a few tunes and that was all.
Was he playing good then? He was playing real good then.
That's right. That was back about 1927. What instrument was he playing?
Clarinet.

Clarinet. He played clarinet. And I can remember playing out at some of the old picnics out at Millenvoig too, Dick. Millenvoig was still going at that time, but it was kind of on the way of fading out at that time. But there were still some pretty good picnics out there. They played some real fine affairs.
They'd have a piano down in the camps? Yeah.
In the camps, uh-huh. Yeah, they had pianos out there. Well, I imagine, Dick, that old jelly roll must have played out there too.
Oh, yeah.
So evidently they had pianos out there in those days.
Who did you play with out there? Do you remember?

Um, well, uh, pick up bands, Dick. Nothing in particular. You know in those days, somebody called you up for a job. You never cared. You didn't much care, no matter who it was. It was just the idea that you had a, you were going to play out at a picnic. And you didn't pay much attention to really who it was. Uh, I remember playing out there with a fellow by name, uh, Early. Played bass. Have you ever taught him that name? Tom Early, yes.
Uh-huh.

He played, he played bass on some of the picnics that I played out there with. Uh, Angie Jumeli played on some of them out there. He played Sousa Porn out there. Uh, some of the trumpet players, I think, were Tony Foucherai. And, uh, Red Bowman, trumpet player. Incidentally, speaking of trumpet players, you must forget, uh, Bill Padron. Bill Padron played fine trumpet. I played with him with the Owls Orchestra, you know. I joined the Owls when they were at the halfway house. That's when Eddie Miller was playing with them. Angelo Palmezano was playing banjo. Frank Neto was playing bass. And Dan LeBlanc was playing tenor sax. Eddie Miller was playing outdoor sax. Dan LeBlanc was playing tenor sax. I didn't know that. Dan LeBlanc was a fine musician. He's a very underrated man. And he also plays wonderful bass too. Sure does. You can hear that. I don't know that. I don't know that. I don't know that.
I don't know that. I don't know that.
I don't know that. I don't know that. I don't know that. You didn't record with them. No, I didn't record with them at the Owls. The Owls.
No, my first records were with Shawkey Banana in 1936 when Shawkey Banana came with me.
He was a very underrated man. And he also plays wonderful bass too. Sure does.
You can hear that on the record. He played great tuba.

Yeah. Very good man. That must have been pretty late then after that. I joined the Owls at the halfway house in 1928 I think it was. And played with them quite awhile. You didn't record with them. No, I didn't record with them at the Owls.
No, I didn't record with them at the Owls.

No, my first records were with Shawkey Banana in 1936 when Shawkey Banana came with them. And we were playing together then. Where is the Shawpery? The Shawpery is now called Maison's Beach House out on Ponchacrine Boulevard. Were the records made in New Orleans? Oh, yes. I made the records with Shawkey at the Roosevelt Hotel. Who was in that band anyway? I think it was Ray Bonitas, Augie Chalang, Myer Wine Boyd, and I was in the band.
And then, I was in the band. Where is the Shawpery?
The Shawpery is now called Maison's Beach House out on Ponchacrine Boulevard.
Were the records made in New Orleans?
Oh, yes. I made the records with Shawkey at the Roosevelt Hotel.
Who was in that band anyway?
I think it was Ray Bonitas, Augie Chalang, Myer Wine Boyd, Julian Langan, Shawkey. I think that was about it.
What did Myer Wine Boyd play? Clarinet.
Of course, he goes in the name of Gene Myers now.
Yeah. He wasn't playing saxes.
Clarinet. Did you have a saxophone playing?
Well, let's see, wait a minute.
I think we had two or three saxes, because Dave Weinstein also played sax. Now, I don't remember whether we had two saxes or three saxes on that section.
And what tunes did you cover?

We did Everybody Loves My Baby, Yes She Do, No She Don't. And then we recorded about six or eight other tunes that were never released. That was really a rough session, because we didn't have air conditioning in those days, and we were hot and bothered, and the piano was all out of tune, and we were recording in one room, and the recording equipment was in another room. It was all set up real bad, you know? We played so long that, of course, everybody's lips were getting bad, and Shawkey's lip was getting bad, and we were all getting...
I want to get back to Dixon in the mist. How did he play on the piano? Did he play more or less legitimately or did he have unusual things?

Well you know, Dixon's piano playing was really amazing because in listening to Dixon's Bix playing piano, I can never really tie in his trumpet with the piano. I don't know if it ever struck you that way, Dick, but listening to his trumpet, it sounds like it's an entirely different phase than his piano playing. His piano sounds so different that it was rhythmical with really sort of modern chords and yet there was the old time flavor along with it. It's just a hard thing to explain, his piano playing. You know, there's a fellow that I'm thinking about right now, Dick. Cy Girard was his name. He used to play saxophone. Cy had a printing company and I was thinking about him. I haven't heard of him for so long. I don't know if anything happened to him or if he's still around town, but if you could get the chance to interview him, I'm sure that he would come up with some real interesting highlights because Cy was one of those kind of people that was around musicians more than he played. And he used to tell me some stories that would really make you laugh, I mean comical things about some of the musicians that he knew. Cy was up in Chicago at the time that the New Orleans Rhythm Kings were up there. And he told me a story about how Bix used to come around a bandstand when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings were playing. And Bix, oh he idolized the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. And after the Rhythm Kings would stop playing and they took a break, Bix used to get up on the piano. And he'd start playing all of these things on the piano and his harmonies were really far advanced, you see. He'd use chords that the Rhythm Kings weren't using. So Paul Merez and Raph and all of these fellas would listen to him playing up there and they'd say, what is this guy playing? What the devil is, what are these, what is he trying to do, you know? So they'd run him off the stand. And this poor guy, Bix was idolizing these fellas to such an extent that he just could stay away from them. But he just could resist playing piano and a couple of times they'd let him sit in. But they said that his piano was just too far away from what they were doing at that time. You see, so that gives you an idea of how far advanced Bix's ideas were on piano. So when he came down here in 1928, Eddie Miller and Monk Hazel and I and I don't know where I think Daniel Blanc was with us, if I'm not mistaken. We were playing together at the time and we went to here, White and St. Charles Theatre. And on the break and intermission with the band while we were in the alleyway or the whatever you call it on the side of the theater there, we were standing up talking to Bix and Frankie Trumbauer. So at that time, Paul Morez was there too. And Paul Morez invited Bix and Trumbauer and Izzy Friedman to play out to his house. So he invited us out too. So that was really a real great evening for me. We played together out there and we were together and Bix played the trumpet and it was really a great, great thrill. So I asked Bix to show me this Bix in a mist that he had recorded at the time because I was trying to get it off the record and the music wasn't published. It was quite a job trying to get it down because it was so intricate, you know, those harmonies. You put it on and you hear one thing and you put it back and you start hearing something else. So Bix said, well, he says, I'll show you. He says, really not as hard as you think. Well, that was really a modest way that he put it, you know. And he sat down and he started showing me some of the spots that I was having trouble with. So as I said, that was a great thrill to me. And as I said, I could never forget that. Did he know the names of the cards? No, he didn't refer to them as names. In other words, he would tell me, here, just do this. And he'd show me a certain passage like the major. He was using so many major, major sevens and 11 chords and things like that. I don't know if Bix even thought of it in terms of what they really want. I don't know. To me, he just played them and that's all. I mean, he didn't worry about what they call them. He just played them and that's it. But he certainly was far ahead with his voicing of his chords as Eddie Connan brought out that he never heard a seventh chord voice the way Bix voiced the seventh chord. Now, whether or not Bix actually thought of it in those terms or not, we don't know. But he certainly did a beautiful job. What about Hardy? Did you ever hear Emmett Hardy? That's the thing that I certainly wish that I had, Dick. No, I never heard Emmett play. I wish I had. Of course, my brother-in-law, Steve Lloyd Cannon, banjo player, he said that he played several times with Emmett Hardy. He said that he certainly was a wonderful cornet player. So I tried to get some ideas as to what style that he played. And Steve says that he certainly played a cornet in a style more or less like a strict New Orleans style of playing. But yet with such a fine tone. Now, Monk Hazel says that it was on the Bix title of Horn. So there again, it's something that you just can't tell because there's two different opinions there. And I respect Monk's opinion because certainly Monk knew Bix's playing. And if he played with Emmett, he certainly knew Emmett's playing. And I respect my brother-in-law Steve's opinion too. So therefore, it's a hard thing to tell. Maybe at some times, Emmett may have sounded like Bix, and then again, maybe at some times he may have played in the vein of King Oliver or Louis or something. It's hard to tell. But he certainly must have been a wonderful cornet player.
Did you ever hear Brownlee's band? Norman Brownlee?

Norman Brownlee? No. No, in fact, Norman Brownlee was at the same session that I told you about at Paul Merez's house. He was out there that night. Yes, I heard Brownlee. Brownlee's band. In fact, several times, I can't say that I can recall anything definite about it or as to what, how good it was or anything like that.
I thought he might have been a piano player that you listened to us.
Well, I believe Norman did play piano, didn't he?
Yes, he was a piano player.
Did he play something else too besides piano? Did he play?
He also plays bass now.
He played bass too, did he?
I don't know whether he played it here, but he plays bass fiddle now too.
What's Norman doing now? Pensacola.
He's in Pensacola?
He's in Pensacola? He's in Pensacola.

He's in Pensacola. He's in Pensacola. Insurance, I think. He was president of the local, but he's still playing piano. Still playing piano. I remember him and I saw him a couple years ago. He plays fine. Still plays fine. We were often stomping.
Who were some of the great cornet players around town when we were on the subject of cornet players too? What do you remember when you were young?
Well, of course, the ones that I played with, I think I've already mentioned, like Bill Gillen and Bill Padron and Abbey Brunas. Let's see, Brent Bowman.
Do you have any particular favorite out of them?

Well, I think they all played very fine. Abbey Brunas played a real good lead swing cornet. Of course, with a more refined sort of tone. Brent Bowman was certainly a real fine driving lead trumpet player at one time. Same as Bill Padron. Bill Padron really played a real fine lead trumpet. In fact, Eddie Miller picked him as his favorite. Eddie Miller was interviewed by a downbeat of Metronome magazine back in 35 or 36, and Eddie Miller picked him as his favorite. lead trumpet player. So, you know, he must have been pretty good. Oh, yeah.
Well, the records show that with Al. That's right. Well, Padron and Bowman both come through good. Yeah, that's right.
Of course, Kid Rene and Petit and all those fellows were around at that time too. They were no slouches either. You remember them?
Yes, I can remember them.
Of course, I wish I could remember Buddy Bowman. I guess a lot of other people do too.
A lot of them remember him and never heard him too. In other words, they have a strong imagination.
Yeah. Well, of course, I heard Bunk.
We don't have to talk.
We don't need to go into him. We know how he played. What did Buddy Petit play? Buddy, maybe I'm getting mixed up. Buddy was a trumpet player, wasn't he? Yeah, he was.
Yeah, that's right. I thought I was getting kind of a little confused for a minute. Of course, naturally, I didn't get to hear those fellows as much as I did with the other

fellows. I didn't get around those fellows as much as I did with those fellows. I thought you, Louis Primo was really good in his early days. I think he played much better than he does now. I played with him at the old club called the Avalon Club in the old days. He was playing quite, playing real good trumpet at that time. He was a real good copy of Louis Armstrong in those days.
When was that?
About the early 30s, I'd say. Yeah, must have been about the early 30s.
What was this Goofus style that they talked about? Goofus style?
Well, it's quite hard to explain it by talking about it, more or less than hearing it or playing it.
Are there any records that you think of as being typically Goofus?
Well, the Goofus Five was a perfect example of that style. I can't remember. I did have a couple of old records by the Goofus Five.
Would be the kind of the Red Nickels group?

Oh, the Red Nickels type. More, yeah. I would say that it leans very strong towards the Red Nickels type of record. They accented. They did like the . You know, they accented. It was a very strong accentuation. They're syncopated style but accenting. They didn't accent the second beat or they didn't the fourth beat as we do in the Strip-Dixieland type of music. It was more or less . I can't sing it as well as I could play it. In those days, if I had a piano here, I could give an example of the accentuation that they used. It was a very, very peculiar style of playing. I say that the Chicago style of music kind of revolved around that quite a bit.
Well, we'll get to a piano or something. You can give me a couple of bars and some of these different things.

You can demonstrate it a lot better than just by humming it. But that was a good point that you brought out because the Goofus style of music was really a very weird, weird style. I think they used that bariton sax, or the bass sax rather, played a very important part in there. And they used to use a little horn called the Goofus horn. Do you remember that thing?
Yeah, I've heard it on the record.

I owned one of those at one time. It was made just like the keys were set up just like a keyboard with little round buttons, you know, that you pressed. And they had a long rubber tube that you blew into. And you could get a sound sort of like a harmonica out of it. And you could really play some real crazy things on it.
Did you play it much?

Yeah, I used to use it. I used it quite a bit when I was playing with Eddie Miller and Bill Padron back in the early 19, in 29, 30. We used to use it quite a lot. In fact, if I dig up one right now and make a record of it, it's a novelty, you know. They have one in the Cabildo.

That's a true, a lot there. What bands played Goofus style in down here? I can't say that I can remember any of the New Orleans bands playing that style. It wasn't too influential. I don't think it was too influential.
I don't think it went over too big with the New Orleans bands down here. I think that was used mostly by the bands up north, you know.
Did you work with Johnny Harmon in those days?

I can't remember too well if I worked any jobs with Johnny in those days. I knew of Johnny and had met him and certainly talked with him many times. I can't recall playing any early jobs with Johnny until our association in 1946 at WSMB radio station.
The Lesley Hems records, they sound like nickels, you know. He made two tunes, I forget the date, but the late 20s, Johnny Harmon's Bayou's
was that when he used this piano player, Horace Dias? Was Horace Dias on some of those records with him?
Yeah.

That is a fine piano player that we left out. Horace Dias, I remember him when I was coming up. Another piano player by the name of, see his name's come to you as you go along, a fellow by the name of Pellegrini, Vic Pellegrini. He was a very fine piano player.
Did he play solo or was he playing solo?

Vic played around with bands, and in fact I think he played with Johnny Detroit if I'm not mistaken. And he used to do a lot of early radio work, solo work. Vic Pellegrini was a very, very fine jazz piano player. I would definitely tell him as a jazz piano player.
What about Diaz?
Horace Dias was a very fine musician and a good piano player and a very good arranger. In fact, I think he's still doing a lot of arranging work for some very fine bands right now.
What happened to him? He's gone.

Oh, well he's up north. I think I asked somebody about him and they said that they had met him and that he was still doing arranging. I think he used to do arranging for Eddie Guchin at one time if I'm not mistaken.
He does a lot of stocks too. Yeah. He played a few of them. Yeah. A lot of all that kind of stuff.

Well, Horace Dias played at the old Silver Slipper when Jink Morton played down there. Which band was this? I was trying to think of the band. Now, I think my brother-in-law Steve Lloyd Cantor had the band. And I know he definitely had him. Steve was on banjo and Horace Dias was on piano. Jink Morton on bass. I can't remember who the clarinet player was and who the trumpet player he had with at that time. But that was a good band of those days too. It was a real good swinging band.
Who were some of the clarinet players you remember as outstanding? We've already mentioned Aaron and now. Harry Shields.

Harry Shields. Bill Bourgeois. Of course, Raymond. Raymond Burke. And then, of course, to get back to piano players, another fine piano player just entered my mind. A little fella that used to play with Raymond at the Club Plantation. Oh, Julia Chavez. Mm-hmm. Julia Chavez was a good, very good, very good jazz piano player. Played very nice style. He played with Raymond quite a while at the, when it was Pete Hoyman's Club Plantation. Henry with Henry Walde. That was a real good little swinging little band. They used to go in and listen to them? Yeah. Oh, they used to come on the air every night in those days. That was back about 30 or 31. Raymond used to play his harmonica. I think they used to use a theme song. Raymond came on with his harmonica solo. Some kind of a real weird, wild solo. But it was a real good little band. Really swung in those days.
Raymond was considered outstanding then?
Raymond was real outstanding then. Boy, he played some wonderful clarinet with him. With his band.
It's funny how he never got recognition until-
Until later years. Until later years. That's right. Well, of course, that's the same old story as the jazz story. So many men that were lost until later years. Bill Bourgeois.
Bill Bourgeois, that's right. He told me how he always missed getting recorded. He would always come last time. That's right.

Let's see. You say you heard rap once, huh? I heard rap once, that's right. Well, of course, there were a lot of good musicians and a lot of good bands. I think at the Hollywood Dance Hall on St. Claude Avenue, that open air dance hall that Shockey and Leon Primer had. That was a good spot there in those days. Back about 32, 33. Fazzola played there. I played with Boz and Scagliona. Boz and Scagliona used to make a real good team.
What would they play? Did you play both?

Well, let's see. I think Gene Meyer was playing, or Meyer Weinboy was playing alto lead. Fazz was playing third sax, I believe, in those days. And Scagliona was playing tenor, if I'm not mistaken. That was a real good band. And Joe Lloyd Cannon was playing bass. Aubrey Schlang played drums. That was a real good spot.
How did that deal work there? Who would have the band in charge? Shawkey.

Leon Primer wasn't playing. I think, in fact, when I joined the band, Primer had gotten out of it. I think at one time, Primer and Shawkey would play together. But at the time that I joined it, I think Shawkey was just playing one trumpet. No trombone.
No trombone.

I think Julian Lane might have played trombone in it. Of course, the trombone I think changed a couple of times, but I think Julian played one time there too. I worked one time too with a little outfit at the Roosevelt Hotel, and Harold Jaudy was the leader. Harold Jaudy played sax there, clarinet. He played, Harold played real good sax and clarinet too.
Who was in that band?

We had Marion Souter on trumpet. I think Red Bowman, I think they had two trumpets. I think we had Shilang on drums again. Von Gammon played drums in Viberhop. What do you call the name of him? Bill Wiley, Bill Wiley I think played guitar. He's not too well known, but he was more of a vocalist, I think.
That's not Henry Wiley's brother, huh?
No, no, this fellow's name was Wiley. Wiley.
Wiley, yeah.
Wiley, yeah. Wiley was the bass player, wasn't he?
Yeah, Bill Wiley was the bass player.
Bill Wiley was, yeah, bass player. Yeah, there's quite a number of things that, jobs and musicians that you meet and encounter in the course of 35 years, you know.
Some of them even have the same name. Exactly, you know. Yeah. Different instrument.

Yeah, that's right. We had a good little band at the original 25 Club. That was back off the Pontchartrain Road where the Honeysuckle Inn was. You may have heard of the Honeysuckle Inn. The Honeysuckle Inn and the original 25 Club were right across from each other. Is that? Sharky opened at the original 25 Club and then left there and went across the street to the Honeysuckle Inn. And I was playing over at the original 25 Club with Eddie Miller and Bill Padron. And I think Sharky was playing over at the other, at the Honeysuckle Inn at that time. It was a real keen rivalry between two places. The boss of the Honeysuckle Inn used to stand out with a lantern because it had no electric light, there was no street lights and they had to use an old lantern. And they had the 25 Club hired a man and they'd both be standing out there with lanterns flagging the cars down as they'd come down the road, you know. So one didn't turn out to a free fall.
There's a place, I think one day I was at the market with Bob Coquille, do you remember that? It was about the original 2 Bits Club, is that the same thing?

The original 2 Bits Club, that's it. That's right. That's what, everything was 25 cents. Did they sell whiskey? No, that was in prohibition days. They couldn't sell whiskey. That's why they charged 25 cents. A bowl of ice was 25, a Coca-Cola was 25. The sandwich was 25 cents. Anything you ordered was 25 cents. And of course if you brought your own bottle of whiskey in, you paid 25 cents for the privilege of bringing in your own whiskey. And they did pretty good business too, even at that. I also played at the Honey Circle Inn, even before these days. I played out there, I believe it was about 26 or 27, with a little band with Steve Massico, and Steve Massico played outdoor sax. Very good. A fellow by the name of Henry Ferriero played banjo, and a fellow by the name of Fitch Flick played drums. And I waited out there for quite a while. That's what I'll take.
So when you made those records with Sharky, were you working with him?

Yeah, that was in 36, I believe. Yeah, Sharky was playing. We had Sharky. I think Leo Brookhoven was playing Fitch trumpet. Sharky was playing second trumpet. We had Adrian Gosley playing drums, and Dan McGowan was playing bass.
This is the time you made the records with Sharky?
This is the time we made them with records.
And you didn't use the same guy?

He didn't use the same band, no. That's funny. Yeah, well you know, it was one of those things, you see, when Deck of Records came through, they wanted Sharky, so naturally I guess he picked out a band that he thought would be better suited for jazz records. And I guess that's the way it went. You had Leo Brookhoven, you say? Leo Brookhoven playing trumpet, Fitch trumpet. And of course we had a full saxophone section, a fellow by the name of Scorsoni playing sax, and Franzella played sax a while out there. And we even had this fellow, Randall. Doc Randall?
Doc Randall? Doc Randall, yeah.

Doc Randall played out there with us a while, before he went north, you know. In fact, Ben Pollack, Ben Pollack used to come out and sit in with us. He was playing at the Blue Room in 1935, and he used to come out there after work, and he'd come and sit in with us. And Glenn Miller, when he first started with his band, used to come out there. Glenn used to, Glenn, in fact, I can remember talking with Glenn Miller quite a bit about his band, and Glenn told me about his big plans that he had for this band. And certainly he was laying the foundation in for what he later made with that swing era, you know. I don't know if Foss was playing with Glenn Miller at the time. But Glenn used to come out there quite often. And Bob Crosby, when he came in town with his band, which was a little bit later, I think around 1936 or 1937. Crosby used to come out there with Ray Badouk and Eddie and Haggard and all of those fellows. I met Bob Zerke at that time, too. He was with Crosby.
I think he still has a tremendous influence on piano players today. Definitely.

Definitely. I think even on some of the modern players he had influence. Because that Roman style that sort of broken style of bass that he used there, octaves and single note figures, surely was a wonderful, very effective style of playing.
How big a breech did he have?

He had a very little hand. His hand was very small. In fact, all of these tenths had to be done with a roll because he could never reach them, just spanning them. I don't know what he could do. I think Bob Zerke probably had trouble spanning an octave. He had such a small hand. But he could sure get over it. He could sure get over it.
Did Glenn Miller sit in with you?
I can never recall Glenn sitting in with the band, but he used to enjoy coming out and listening to us at that time. I don't know what I wanted to ask you.
Did you have a guitar player on those deck of records at the shop?

I don't believe me. Not that I can recall. My brother-in-law, Freddie, was playing guitar with us at the chaperie at the time. But I know he didn't play on the record and I don't remember of any guitar player playing on those records with us. I think we just had drums, bass and piano.
Mr. Bob, a couple minutes.

Well, of course that brought us up to pretty much up to the time of 1946 when all the revival of jazz came back. From there on, why it was really, I guess a story that everybody's been talking about now.
When did you start playing solo so much?

I started playing solo piano by 41 or 42 and then I was drafted in draft, not drafted, I enlisted in the U.S. Maritime Service and played with a little nine piece band all the two years of 1943, 44, and 45. I played with a nice little band. Had some fellas from Tommy Tucker's band. Billy Newboyga on drums. Nina Baconi on sax. Johnny Senac on bass.
How far away did you get away from your city?
Well, you know, dick me, I've never been out of New Orleans in my life. I don't live over 150 miles and all through the war I was only 60 miles. That's about as far as I ever got.
That's fun. Do you have an office to play with big bands away from here?

Yeah, I had quite a bit of office. One time I had an offer from Joe Venuti when he was in town here. And, of course, I had several individual offerings out of town at different clubs that hang over in San Francisco. They wanted me out there a couple of times. Joe Delaney wanted to vote for me in New York just recently. But I never could make up my mind. In fact, not that I could make up my mind, circumstances just wouldn't let me go. So here I am still in New Orleans.
Well, I think that just about finishes it off for a day. We'll have to come back again for the time, huh? Alright. It's fine, man. It's good. .
